data.explanation: The move g4 pursues an aggressive plan of kingside pawn storm, aiming to open lines towards the enemy king and intensify the attack, which is sharper but leaves behind weak squares if the assault stalls. In contrast, castling long with O-O-O reflects a quieter, safer approach, prioritizing king safety and simplified position, but it concedes a small material deficit and commits the king to a particular flank, possibly inviting targeted attacks. Playing Bc4 adopts a strategy of simplification by exchanging pieces early, reducing complexity and chasing activity on equal terms; it is more cautious than the pawn storm but still concedes some winning chances if the opponent's chances rely on maintaining more pieces on the board. The pawn storm, while riskier, offers greater dynamism and potential attacking payoffs but at the cost of structural weaknesses and a shift of the king to the queenside. The castling move is more conservative, focusing on safety and gradual development, with a slight concession to material and position. The choice depends on the player's style: the pawn storm is for those seeking sharp, attacking play, accepting risk, while castling is for those who prefer safety and quiet maneuvering, conceding some initiative. The simplification plan is a balanced, cautious approach, focusing on clear exchanges and endgame stability.

data.detectedBy: Material (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9) after the line's exchanges settle is two or more points better than at the start.

data.title: Push the passed pawn
data.meaning: A pawn with no enemy pawn able to stop it advances. In an endgame this is usually the whole game; in a middlegame it ties the opponent's pieces to blockading it.
data.rightWhen: When the pawn is supported and the squares in front of it are not firmly blockaded.
data.concedes: A pawn pushed too far without support becomes a target.
data.detectedBy: One of the side to move's pawn moves lands on a square with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its own or either neighbouring file.

data.title: Kingside pawn storm
data.meaning: The f-, g- and h-pawns advance at the enemy king to pry open lines to it. Classically with the kings castled on opposite wings, where the pawns in front of your own king do not move.
data.rightWhen: Kings on opposite wings, the centre closed or stable, and more pieces able to join the attack than can defend.
data.concedes: The storming pawns can never come back. If the attack stalls, the squares behind them are weak — and with kings castled on the SAME side, it loosens your own king too.
data.detectedBy: Middlegame material; the enemy king ends the line on the kingside; the side to move plays two pawn moves on the f-h files, or one if the kings end on opposite wings.

data.title: Queenside pawn storm
data.meaning: The a-, b- and c-pawns advance at an enemy king castled queenside.
data.rightWhen: The mirror of the kingside storm: opposite-side castling with the opponent's king on the queenside.
data.concedes: As the kingside storm: the pawns cannot come back, and a stalled storm leaves holes.
data.detectedBy: Middlegame material; the enemy king ends the line on the queenside; two pawn moves on the a-c files, or one with the kings on opposite wings.

data.title: Minority attack
data.meaning: Two queenside pawns (typically b4-b5) advance against three, not to break through but to exchange and leave the opponent with a weak, backward or isolated pawn — the classic plan in the Carlsbad structure of the Queen's Gambit Exchange.
data.rightWhen: When you have fewer queenside pawns than the opponent and their king is not there — a slow, positional plan.
data.concedes: Time. It is slow, and the opponent's counterplay is usually on the kingside or in the centre (a knight to e4, a kingside attack).
data.detectedBy: Middlegame material; the side to move starts with fewer pawns on the a-c files than the opponent; it pushes its b-pawn; the enemy king is not on the queenside.

data.title: Sacrifice for the initiative
data.meaning: Material is given up — two or more points once the exchanges settle — and the engine still rates the line as good. What comes back is time, open lines or a weakened king.
data.rightWhen: When the engine's score says the compensation is real. The score is the evidence; the material count alone would call it a blunder.
data.concedes: The material, permanently, if the initiative runs out.
data.detectedBy: Settled material is two or more points WORSE for the side to move, and the line is not a forced mate.

data.title: Central break
data.meaning: A pawn on the c-, d-, e- or f-file strikes at an enemy pawn to open the centre on your own initiative.
data.rightWhen: When your pieces are better placed than the opponent's for an open position, or their king is still in the centre.
data.concedes: Tension. Once opened, the centre stays open, and a break made too early can leave an isolated or hanging pawn.
data.detectedBy: A pawn move by the side to move, landing on the c-f files, that captures an enemy pawn or attacks one — excluding a recapture of a pawn that arrived on the previous move, which answers the opponent's break.

data.title: Prepare the centre
data.meaning: A pawn move that covers the square in front of your own central pawn, so that pawn can advance later: f3 behind e3 to prepare e4, c4 beside d4 to contest d5.
data.rightWhen: Before a central break, when making it immediately would fail.
data.concedes: A tempo, and sometimes a loosened king position (f3 especially).
data.detectedBy: A non-capturing pawn move that attacks an empty square on the c-f files directly in front of one of the side to move's own pawns.

data.title: Simplify
data.meaning: Exchanges — four or more captures in the first ten plies, or the queens coming off. Right when ahead, or when the opponent's activity depends on pieces that can be traded.
data.rightWhen: When you are better in the endgame than the middlegame: a better pawn structure, a better minor piece, material up.
data.concedes: Winning chances, if you are the one who needed pieces on the board to attack.
data.detectedBy: Four or more captures by either side in the first ten plies, or both queens gone.

data.title: Gain space on the kingside
data.meaning: Kingside pawns advance without an enemy king to aim at — space, a clamp on squares, or preparing f4/f5 or g4/g5 levers.
data.rightWhen: When the kingside is where your pieces are and theirs are cramped.
data.concedes: The same holes a storm leaves, without the attack to justify them — and often your own king's cover.
data.detectedBy: Middlegame material; two pawn moves on the f-h files; not a storm (the enemy king is not on the kingside).

data.title: Gain space on the queenside
data.meaning: Queenside pawns advance without an enemy king there and without the pawn count that makes it a minority attack — usually a majority advancing to create a passed pawn.
data.rightWhen: With a queenside majority, or to cramp pieces the opponent has put there.
data.concedes: Squares behind the advancing pawns.
data.detectedBy: Middlegame material; two pawn moves on the a-c files; neither a storm nor a minority attack.

data.title: Activate the king
data.meaning: In an endgame the king is a strong piece: it walks towards the centre or the pawns.
data.rightWhen: When the queens are off and mating threats are gone.
data.concedes: Very little — unless the queens are still on, which is why this is only read in queenless positions.
data.detectedBy: The queens were off at the start and the side to move makes two or more king moves in the first ten plies.

data.title: King safety first
data.meaning: Castling now, or next move, before doing anything else: getting the king out of the centre and connecting the rooks.
data.rightWhen: When the centre may open, or when the opponent's pieces are pointing at your uncastled king.
data.concedes: It commits the king to one wing, which tells the opponent where to attack.
data.detectedBy: The side to move castles with its first or second move of the line.

data.title: Prophylaxis
data.meaning: A quiet move that stops the opponent's idea before it starts: a king step to b1 or h1 off a dangerous diagonal, or a3/h3 to take a square from an enemy piece.
data.rightWhen: When the opponent's best plan is clear and yours can wait a move.
data.concedes: A tempo, spent on not losing rather than on winning.
data.detectedBy: The first move is a quiet king move (not castling), or a single-square a- or h-pawn move that is not part of a storm — with queens on the board.

data.title: Development
data.meaning: Knights and bishops come off the back rank. In the opening this is most of the plan.
data.rightWhen: In the opening, and whenever a minor piece is still at home.
data.concedes: Nothing, usually — the question is only which piece and to which square.
data.detectedBy: The first move develops a knight or bishop from the back rank, or the line develops two minor pieces.

data.title: Improve the pieces
data.meaning: Quiet piece moves — a rook to an open file, a knight rerouted to a better square. The position is not ready for a pawn plan, so the pieces go to where they will be needed.
data.rightWhen: When the pawn structure is set and neither side has a break ready.

data.rightWhen: Quiet, balanced positions.
data.concedes: Nothing in particular — which is what makes these positions hard.

data.title: Central break
data.exampleLine: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nxc6 bxc6 Bd3 d5 e5 Nd7 O-O Nc5 f4 g6 Be3 Nxd3 cxd3 c5 Nc3
data.meaning: A pawn on the c-, d-, e- or f-file strikes at an enemy pawn to open the centre on your own initiative.
data.rightWhen: When your pieces are better placed than the opponent's for an open position, or their king is still in the centre.
data.concedes: Tension. Once opened, the centre stays open, and a break made too early can leave an isolated or hanging pawn.

data.title: Prepare the centre
data.exampleLine: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 d5 Bg5 Be7 Nc3 h6 Bxf6 Bxf6 e3 c6 Bd3 dxc4 Bxc4
data.meaning: A pawn move that covers the square in front of your own central pawn, so that pawn can advance later: f3 behind e3 to prepare e4, c4 beside d4 to contest d5.
data.rightWhen: Before a central break, when making it immediately would fail.
data.concedes: A tempo, and sometimes a loosened king position (f3 especially).

data.concedes: Nothing, usually — the question is only which piece and to which square.

data.explanation:
The move e4 is the sharpest choice, pursuing a central break to open the position quickly. This plan concedes tension and aims to distort the pawn structure early, offering opportunities for active piece play but also risking overextension or weakening of the king position. It’s a style-driven approach that favors dynamic play.

Playing d4, on the other hand, adopts a quieter, stable approach focused on central control and development. It aims to prepare the centre patiently without forcing the issue, accepting a slight loss of tempo for a more secure structure, but it leaves the position less open immediately.

Nf3 also aims at central control and development, but it’s slightly more natural and flexible. Like d4, it favors gradual improvement and piece placement over sharpness, aligning with a less risky, more positional style.

Moving e3 is more subdued, reinforcing central control but at the cost of tempo and flexibility, potentially loosening the king’s position. It’s a more restrained, positional approach.

Finally, c4 signals active piece development, particularly knights and bishops, without directly challenging the centre immediately. It is less sharp than e4, more about piecemeal improvement, and concedes nothing substantial but develops quietly.

Overall, e4 is the most aggressive, offering sharp chances at the expense of structural tension; d4 and Nf3 are quieter, aiming for steady development and control; e3 and c4 balance between quiet preparation and piece activity, with e3 being the most subdued. The choice depends on whether the player prefers sharp, tactical play or steady, positional growth.
